faqs.a: If your current savings plus their growth already reaches the goal, the answer is zero — congratulations. Otherwise, check whether a lower goal, a longer timeline, or a slightly higher return assumption closes the gap.

faqs.a: Longer timelines and higher returns both shrink the monthly amount, but the return is uncertain while time is free. Extending the timeline by a year or two is usually the safest lever.
faqs.q: Does a longer timeline or a higher return help more?

howItWorks: This calculator works backwards from your target. It first grows your current savings forward at the expected return, then figures out how much of the goal is still missing. That shortfall is converted into a monthly deposit using the future-value-of-annuity formula, which accounts for the fact that each monthly deposit also earns returns for the months remaining after you make it.

The result shows three numbers: the monthly deposit you need, the total you will put in yourself, and how much investment growth contributes. Seeing the growth share is often the motivating part — over long timelines it can cover a third or more of the goal.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. Returns are not guaranteed, and this calculator ignores inflation, taxes, and fees. For short-term goals where you cannot risk a market dip, run the numbers with a 0% return to see the safe monthly amount.
intro: Work out the monthly deposit you need to reach a savings goal. Enter your target amount, what you have saved, the expected annual return, and how many years you have — the calculator finds the monthly savings that gets you there.

mistakes.text: A 5% annual return is 0.004167 per month, not 0.05. Using the annual rate monthly would make growth look twelve times too strong.
mistakes.title: Using the annual rate as the monthly rate

mistakes.text: Your existing savings keep earning returns the whole time. In the example above, the $5,000 starting amount grows to $6,416.79 on its own, which cuts the monthly deposit.
mistakes.title: Forgetting your starting savings earn interest

mistakes.text: Market returns are uncertain, and a goal you cannot miss — like a house deposit — should be planned with a conservative or 0% return, not the most optimistic one.
mistakes.title: Counting on a high return for a must-hit goal

mistakes.text: $50,000 in five years is not $50,000 of spending power if prices rise. At 3% inflation it buys what about $43,000 buys today, so consider aiming a little higher.
mistakes.title: Ignoring inflation on the goal
